public_rationale: The tribunal record supports the central factual claim: the chatbot incorrectly advised that a customer could seek a retroactive bereavement fare reduction through a refund application. Marcus's wording compresses that into trips being refunded. The evidence establishes a partial refund representation, not a promise to reimburse the entire trip. It also establishes incorrect advice without establishing that an LLM generated it.
limitations: Support depends on reading refunded as including a partial refund and hallucinated as a description of incorrect policy information.
The record does not establish the chatbot's technical architecture.

from_speaker: telling a customer that bereavement trips would be refunded
our_interpretation: The plain reading is that the chatbot incorrectly told a customer they could obtain a refund through Air Canada's bereavement policy after purchasing travel.
Refund includes a partial refund through a reduced fare. The wording does not expressly claim that the chatbot promised reimbursement of the entire trip.
Hallucinated is read as giving invented or incorrect policy information. Establishing the chatbot's architecture or the technical cause of the error is a separate question.
The target is the past customer interaction described in the post. Its date is unspecified in the supplied text, so the interval has no asserted start and ends on the post date.
This concerns the content of customer advice, not a measure of Air Canada's finances.
